name: Starfish extract
lead: Starfish extract is a preparation from the tissues of sea stars, listed in some Korean beauty products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient. Starfish are known for regrowing lost arms, and some researchers study their tissues for regenerative bioactive molecules.[1][2]
Published evidence is very limited: a 2016 zebrafish study and a few patents. No human trial of starfish extract on skin was found.

paras: A 2016 Scientific Reports study amputated arms of Archaster typicus starfish, fractionated their regenerating tissue and tested the fractions on cell wound-healing assays and on lower-jaw regeneration in zebrafish; hexane fractions promoted cell proliferation and migration.[1] A 1984 Japanese paper described biological activity of a starfish extract on human neutrophils.[3] Korean patents describe a fermentation method for a hangover agent and an extract said to suppress UV-induced cell mutation.[4][5]
Wikipedia notes that some starfish regrow arms and that body-wall saponins act as chemical defences whose pharmacological potential is under study.[2]
No studies found. The research above is in cells and zebrafish, and patents are not clinical evidence.

card.summary: A K-beauty marine ingredient inspired by starfish regeneration, supported only by a zebrafish study and patents.

quick.overview:
Starfish extract appears in some Korean skin-care products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient, drawing on starfish's ability to regrow limbs.

Only cell and zebrafish research and patents exist; no human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: In one study, fractions from regenerating starfish tissue boosted cell proliferation and migration in wound-healing assays.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that some starfish contain saponins and, in certain species, toxins, though cosmetic extracts were not addressed.
